Mr. Chairman, the American government's decision to cut down by 15 per cent its imports of Canadian oil is so much on a par with the Canadian Prime Minister's decision to cut down by 15 per cent our United States purchases that we cannot help feeling that one is a direct consequence of the other. As I see it, this will go on and on and, as a result, Canadian trade will be increasingly reduced.
By inviting British industry to mix sentimentality with publicity in Anglo-Canadian relations, for the purpose of drumming up trade, the Minister of Trade and Commerce follows up the suggestion made by the Prime

Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to shift to the United Kingdom 15 per cent of our American imports. Recent developments have shown what harm can be caused by mixing sentiment with business.
However, due to the strategy used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce during election time, Canada was already used to sentimentality. Time will show that the Conservative party lacks the objective approach and that, unfortunately, it has placed party interests above those of the country.
This visit in England, not to sell but to buy goods, proves it beyond doubt. It is not very often that commercial delegations are sent out to buy. If the mission was a success- and probably was for England-we are not so sure it was a success for Canada. We have many reasons to doubt the success of this mission which could hurt our trade with the United States and our export trade as a whole.
I should like to point out some of the reasons for doubting of the success of this mission from the point of view of Canada.
1.	The United States being our main export outlet, anti-American propaganda might be rather harmful to our exporters particularly to those of our farmers whose sales to the American market reach $300 million annually.
2.	Canada's foreign trade shows an unfavourable balance. Increasing our imports from the United Kingdom, even by shifting some of our trade from the United States, will be no solution at all to our trade deficit problem.
3.	In wanting to increase by all means our purchases from the United Kingdom, the Canadian government runs the risk of adversely affecting Canadian industry.
4.	Great Britain's policy is primarily to serve its own interests. We cannot blame her for it. But this fact should enlighten us on the prospects of a sentimental rapprochement with Great Britain. Even if the idea of diverting part of our trade is excellent, I do believe that this question of trade with Great Britain should be dealt with on a business basis. However, I blame the government for adopting a sentimental approach to this matter.
5.	Canadian and British currencies are not interchangeable, whereas Canadian and American dollars are interchangeable. Mind you, the unconvertibility of sterling was decided by Great Britain to protect her own currency and her own trade, which put Canada in a very embarrassing situation and caused our getting closer to the United States.

Now, Mr. Chairman, the former government was aware of our unfavourable trade balance with the United States, and it was just as resolved as the present administration to diversify our purchases and our sales. In any well organized country, that is a perfectly normal thing to do, but the only difference, I think, between the two governments is that the present one has approached this problem with a great deal of brutality and lack of diplomacy, whereas the Liberal party was trying to solve it through diplomatic channels. As a result we now have a commercial policy which tends to drive Canada and the United States farther apart, and which will provide arguments to American protectionists to use against us in Congress.
We know perfectly well that the Hyde Park agreements, signed a few years ago by the Canadian and American governments, were founded on understanding and cordial relations. In any event, that is the only way to solve our difficulties with the United States. We know too that those agreements provided a basis for the prosperity of this country and its wartime and postwar economic expansion.
Whether we like it or not, for geographic and economic reasons, we are called upon to deal increasingly with the United States. The present government's mistake-a mistake which has led us into our present difficulties and will make them worse in the future- was to forget about the time-honoured rule of diplomacy, which should apply not only in external affairs, but in the field of commerce as well.
I hope that an American government will come into power which, like its predecessor in 1939, will understand that economic problems cannot be divorced from political issues and that, if peace is to be made secure, economic, military and political matters must be given equal importance.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to draw a particular matter to the attention of the Minister of Transport and I do so even though I am aware that some arrangements are being made to attempt to overcome the problem which exists on the coast of British Columbia. I raise the matter at this time to make the minister more familiar with the problem that exists there so we can have the best possible arrangement made to meet the problem.
Yesterday the official stopping took place of the passenger service operated by Union Steamships Limited on the coast of British Columbia. We have had knowledge for some

Interim Supply
few weeks now of the intention of this company to stop its passenger service serving the entire coastal area of British Columbia and we also know that through the Canadian maritime commission some activity has taken place to do something about it. I do not know how many hon. members realize and indeed I do not know whether the Minister of Transport himself is familiar with the serious effect that this will have if it is allowed to continue on the many coastal communities that over the years have become dependent on Union Steamships Limited for both passenger and freight service.
This particular company has been in existence since 1889 and every year since then has been servicing the up-coast points with its terminus being in Vancouver. It affects so many communities to a greater or lesser degree that it would take up too much time of the committee to attempt to enumerate the various communities and describe the manner in which they would be affected and the number of people in each community who will be affected. However, I have received a number of telegrams from various community organizations and individuals in that part of British Columbia and I am sure other hon. members have received telegrams of a similar type. In order to give you a brief indication of the effect this stoppage and curtailment of service will have and the diversity of interests that are involved I would like to mention just one or two comments in the telegrams and relate the source of these wires.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if my hon. friend would permit me to bring to his attention some very recent developments of which he perhaps may not be aware. The government is well aware of this matter and negotiations are under way at the present time in the hope of providing a substitute service.

I appreciate the comments of the Minister of Finance in that regard, Mr. Chairman. You may recall that we inquired today of the Minister of Transport about this matter and received the answer that we would have a detailed statement on Monday about the result of the negotiations and what the status is at the present time and what the future type of service will be. As I mentioned earlier, I want to place these remarks on Hansard even though the Minister of Transport is not here so that he may be a little more familiar with the situation than he may be at the moment and therefore be in a position to make the best possible

arrangements for the continuation and extension of the service that was in existence up until yesterday and I hope you will allow me to proceed in this fashion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is evidently no possibility of persuading the present carrier to continue the service that has existed heretofore.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I gathered that from private discussions. However, we are not too concerned with the present carrier providing service so long as the service is provided by someone else. If, as the minister says, the government has full knowledge of the situation undoubtedly the Minister of Transport has received similar telegrams and letters from individuals and communities and I expect I could dispense with that phase of it. I would go on to point out that these people are not particularly concerned with the present carrier continuing to provide this service but they are concerned that some service be made available to them so they will not become completely isolated as will be the case for many of them if something concrete and definite is not done.
At the moment we only know that some arrangements are being made. We do not know what those arrangements are and we will not know until Monday. We cannot know at the moment whether those arrangements will be suitable. I can guess that they will not be as extensive, on the same level or with the same regularity as the service that was provided previously by Union Steamships Limited.
I wish to draw attention to some of the other aspects of this question of transportation on the coast of British Columbia. My remarks in this regard are not confined to Union Steamships Limited or to some other company which might provide a similar type of service, that is a marine passenger service, to these communities, but are directed to the general question of transportation in the coastal area of British Columbia. Before going on to discuss this I think I am entitled to raise the question as to why Union Steamships Limited gave notice a few weeks ago of its intention to stop this service on January 2.
An interesting and lengthy advertisement was placed in the Prince Rupert Daily News on Saturday, December 21 announcing the curtailment of service and I wish to refer to one or two paragraphs rather than the complete context of the advertisement. The advertisement reads in part as follows:
Our representations in this current situation have been in Ottawa in complete detail for some time, and Ottawa has been equally well informed for a

number of years that the passenger services to coastal points were becoming increasingly costly to operate.
I assume that by "Ottawa" reference is made to the federal government. The following paragraph in the advertisement reads:
We are informed by Ottawa that subsidy sufficient to cover costs is not possible at this time and we are therefore regretfully forced to make this decision.
Knowing Union Steamships Limited as I do I know they have a "tongue in cheek" attitude when they say they are regretfully forced to to do something of this nature. The general thought behind the particular paragraph I read is designed to leave the impression that the federal government is at fault for the company having to curtail its freight service and stop its passenger service. It makes reference to subsidy. Other references have been made to this particular subsidy or subvention in this house in time past. As I understand it almost since the turn of the century the federal government has granted subsidies to this particular company to service some of the more remote parts of the coast of British Columbia. In my opinion the advertisement placed here by Union Steamships Limited, designed, as I am sure it is, to show that the present Conservative government rather than the company is at fault for the curtailment of service, is completely false and leaves an inaccurate impression in the minds of the people who are affected by this action. So far as I am concerned it is an attempt in the first instance by Union Steamships Limited to get a larger subsidy than it has been receiving in past years.
I am sure that this curtailment of their service was merely another little part of the game of attempting to blackmail the federal authorities into granting them a higher subsidy and in the process use the people in the various small and large communities on the coast of British Columbia as pawns in the game. I should like to make reference to another part of this advertisement which relates to the subsidy. It reads as follows:
The matter of Union Steamships' subsidy is public knowledge as the subject has been critically brought to the floor of the House of Commons by a British Columbia member on several occasions.
Of course, they do not do the hon. member the courtesy of mentioning his name but I am sure we all know to whom they refer. I do not think I would be going too far afield in saying that the hon. member is familiar to all of us. I am sure it is the hon. member for New Westminster to whom the Union Steamships refer in this particular advertisement who has, I understand from my reading of Hansard, raised the question of this subsidy critically and bitterly on the 96698-178

floor of the House of Commons while at the same time a navigation company, a competitor of the Union Steamships Company on the coast of British Columbia, was complaining just as bitterly to the Canadian maritime commission about the same subsidy. The name of that particular company is Northland Navigation Limited. This company has raised the greatest amount of fuss about this subsidy with the federal authorities and the maritime commission.
Suggestions have been made both in and out of the house that the granting of this subsidy by the previous administration to Union Steamships Limited had some political connotation. This undoubtedly arises from the fact that one of the hon. members in the other place is the president of Union Steamships Limited and has been so for probably two or three years. Whether there is any substance to the criticism that because the president of the company was of the same political complexion as the previous government he therefore was able to get more favourable consideration than other companies might get or not I do not know. Frankly, personally, I doubt very much whether that was the case. However, it has been raised; it has been questioned not by myself but by another member of this house that this is the reason why Union Steamships Limited have received this particular subsidy, and accordingly the service should be put on a competitive basis so that other companies who wanted to might be able to bid for that passenger subsidy.
As I said, one of the most vociferous companies was Northland Navigation which operate a freight service on the coast of British Columbia. It is perfectly fine to say that there must be bids and that people who can provide the best type of service should be the ones to get the subsidy on an open bid basis. That is a justifiable and a decent approach to the question of getting a subsidy. The only exception that one could take to that is that Northland Navigation Company,, which raised all the fuss and the noise about the subsidy for passenger service, were themselves not able at that time, and are still not able, to provide any passenger service. They are in the freight service business. I feel justified in raising this question. There may be some political connotations to the fact that Northland Navigation has raised this issue and the fact that they were supported in their complaint by the hon. member for New Westminster. It is unfortunate that he is not in his place today because I am sure we would appreciate his thoughts and remarks on this matter.

There is a gentleman in the province of British Columbia by the name of Mr. Einar Gunderson who is known to some of us. Einar Gunderson was for one short period the minister of finance in the Social Credit administration in the province of British Columbia. Besides his many other private concerns, Mr. Gunderson is interested in and is also a director of Northland Navigation Limited, and is concerned probably from that point of view.
While we are talking about the question of Northland Navigation and one of its directors, Einar Gunderson, complaining about competition and not being able to bid for a subsidy granted by this federal government and the previous government for passenger service on the coast of British Columbia, we should have a brief look at some of the activities of the Northland Navigation Company as they apply to competition.
In British Columbia, as many people know, we have a liquor control board. From time to time beer and liquor are shipped through the liquor control board from the breweries or the distilleries to up-coast points for sale and distribution. Ever since Northland Navigation entered the picture of freight shipping, ever since Einar Gunderson became a director of the company, wherever Union Steamships-and I couple these two companies together because I am familiar with them-and Northland Navigation provided freight service to the same points, Northland Navigation now and ever since Mr. Gunderson became a director have the exclusive right to transport and ship and bring the liquor from the points in Vancouver up to the various up-coast points. Where Union Steamships used to transport some of this freight at one time they now are completely shut out and are not able to bid on the shipping of liquor to these particular spots. If the question of the free competitive spirit, as it is loosely referred to, applies in one instance, with respect to the payment of a subsidy, then certainly it should apply in the other field of shipments. Whether politics are being played there is for other people to speculate on and not for me.
The entire history of transportation services on the coast of British Columbia for many years now shows that every community-and there are many hundreds of them-every logging camp, every pulp mill, every small, isolated spot from the southern tip of British Columbia to the Alaska border, in every instance has been at the mercy of some fly-bynight corporation or company either in the air transport or the marine transport field. Anybody who has had any familiarity with

it will know that that is the absolute truth. Over the years we have seen all sorts of small, two-bit airline companies with a couple of Seabees, trying to get into the show and make a few dollars by providing some sort of service. They have been providing a type of service which leaves much to be desired. We have seen on the coast of British Columbia, because some of those concerns were not able to give good, safe service, many air disasters. Many people have been killed because small air lines have been either unable or unwilling to provide a safe type of passenger service to some of those up-coast points.
We have also seen exactly the same thing taking place in the marine transporation field. Companies have started operations with a few small boats here and there and have attempted to provide some sort of service to the up-coast points but have met with the same disastrous results. People in small communities from one end of the country to the other have been subjected to the disastrous effects of the operations of these small concerns. Some years ago we could see the situation which now exists developing. Probably it will continue to exist to a lesser degree after we are informed on Monday about the arrangements which were mentioned today.
We have seen this situation coming even in the case of the large companies. People from one end of the coast to the other are at the mercy of private corporations who are more concerned about how many dollars they can milk from the people and stow away in their pockets than they are in providing service for the people who have to travel up and down the coast. It is time that we took a longer look at the question of transportation on the coast of British Columbia. The Union Steamships situation has merely brought the matter to a head. It is time that we established some sort of all-inclusive transportation system, some agency for coordinating all forms of transportation on the coast.
Probably the most effective way that could be done would be through a crown corporation in the transportation field on the coast of British Columbia. Such a corporation would provide air passenger and freight service and marine passenger and freight service. As a crown corporation dedicated to providing service primarily it would be in a position, depending on weather, economic and other factors, to alternate between air and marine service. There is some discussion at the present time about airline companies being able to move in where Union Steamships is moving out.

That is only possible to a limited degree. At this time of the year it is very hazardous to attempt to travel by air along the coast of British Columbia except in some of the larger aircraft that follow beams and land at adequate airports. Many times days and days are spent waiting for the weather to break so that people may get in or out.
On the other hand, marine transportation generally is not upset by weather conditions on the coast of British Columbia. I hope that by placing these suggestions on the record the Minister of Transport will be able to understand the situation a little better and will have the benefit of another point of view. In his endeavours to meet the situation I trust he will not be confined to making another deal with a private company which will have to be subsidized and I hope he will not leave the residents up and down the coast of British Columbia in the hands and at the mercy of another private corporation. It is time to co-ordinate and bring together the different forms of transportation so that the people will be provided with an adequate year round freight and passenger service by one form of transportation or another and will not be left, as they have been for the past 50 or 60 years, at the mercy of the immediate economic outlook of a private corporation.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join the hon. member for Skeena in saying a few words about the coastal transportation situation in the province of British Columbia. In view of the interjection by the Minister of Finance a few moments ago, I should like to say at the outset that this is a matter which should concern not only his colleague, the Minister of Transport, but every member of the government. Perhaps I should put the situation in such a manner that the Minister of Finance will appreciate its significance as far as the people of the coast of British Columbia are concerned.
I can well imagine that if the Canadian Pacific railway had made an announcement a few weeks ago that effective on January 2 it would discontinue its passenger services between Montreal and Vancouver a good many members of the house would have been expressing some concern about the situation and that even if an announcement was made by the Minister of Transport, as he did today with respect to the matter we are discussing, that negotiations were going on for the provision of an alternate service, the mere fact such a statement had been made would not set the minds of members of the house completely at ease. The fact remains that if the Minister of Transport had got up and 96698-1784

told us that negotiations were being conducted with some other concern to provide an alternative service between Montreal and Vancouver such an announcement would have been greeted with a certain amount of understandable scepticism.
While the hon. member for Skeena and myself are undoubtedly awaiting with a good deal of interest the announcement which the Minister of Transport said he would make on Monday, nevertheless we are perfectly aware of the fact, in the light of our understanding of what he has been doing, that whatever the announcement may be it will not mean a complete solution of the problems that the hon. member for Skeena has been discussing. As the hon. member for Skeena said, this is not a matter which has cropped up suddenly overnight. The action of Union Steamships in discontinuing all passenger services has perhaps brought the matter to wider attention than was the case before because not only are most of the smaller communities on the coast affected but also a good many of the larger ones.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in order to give the Minister of Finance and the members of the present government some indication that this is a problem which has been in existence for some time and has been brought to the attention of the house from time to time, perhaps I might be permitted to refer to certain speeches on the subject which I have made in the house on former occasions. I have a few volumes of Hansard on my desk, and I find in checking back that on November 30, 1953, the occasion of the very first speech I ever made in the house, I had this to say as recorded on page 461 of Hansard:
We have a situation now where, almost without notice, steamer services are being withdrawn or reduced. People are worrying. Those who have been on the islands for the last 30 years* or more are suddenly left without the means of getting in their supplies.
I went on to say:
Of course we cannot overlook the impact of air travel upon the facilities that can be provided by a coastal steamship service. Certainly no one would suggest that the advantages of air travel should be removed from those people. It seems to me a revolution is taking place in the whole transportation set-up in that coastal area ... I believe it is a matter to which the government should be giving very careful study and attention at this time.
There is a need for the development of an overall and co-ordinated policy in respect of the type of services that can be supplied to and maintained for the people on the coast. I think some study must be made as to how those services can be co-ordinated, keeping in mind possible highway developments . . .
I go on to explain that that of course would involve the authority and responsibility of the provincial government of British

Columbia. I suggest there is a great deal of similarity between the remarks I made back in 1953 and the remarks that have just been made by the hon. member for Skeena. I, too, have had a great number of telegrams in the last week or so. I can only say this, in discussing them briefly, that they bear a remarkable similarity, except they may be coming from somewhat different communities, to the telegrams and letters I was receiving back in 1953 when I made that speech.
Later on in that session we were discussing the estimates of the Department of Transport, and when we were discussing provisions for subsidized services I had some remarks to make which I addressed to the then minister of transport, the Hon. Lionel Chevrier. I said then, as found at page 5866 of Hansard for June 11, 1954:
So as to complete the general picture as I see it, calculations I make would indicate that for the Atlantic coast of Canada provisions in the estimates by way of operating deficits and subventions seem to total $7,810,725, whereas, so far as I have been able to discover, for the Pacific coast of Canada at the present time we are being asked to provide the modest sum of $345,000.
I am not rising in my place to ask that the amount for the Pacific coast be increased to equal that for the Atlantic, or anything like that; but I do feel the situation is one concerning which the Department of Transport and the federal government could take effective action, if they would. If I were going to put my remarks in the form of a question to the minister I suppose I would ask him whether if Vancouver island were to revert to the status it once had, when it was a separate entity from British Columbia, the federal government would then be willing to consider accepting some of the responsibilities, which apparently they do accept in respect of another island described, so the easterners tell me, as "the island" on the Atlantic coast, just as we term Vancouver island "the island" on the Pacific coast.
The Minister of Transport, as so often happens, tried to prevent the development of an extended debate on this subject, and had this to say:
X would not want my hon. friends from the west coast, or the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, to think that his area of the country is being overlooked. It is not. But the consideration has to be in one case by way of subsidy, and in the other by way of the fulfilment of a commitment. And I hope he will not take from that any suggestion that we are not anxious to give sympathetic consideration to any application made for additional transportation service on the west coast, or to and from Vancouver island.
At that point the member for Kamloops, now the Minister of Justice, entered the discussion and he had this to say:
I have no desire to provoke a debate, but I could not allow the minister's remarks to go by without making the observation that the provision of transportation facilities was also a term of entering confederation at the time British Columbia entered. The minister will be aware that there has been a controversy, perhaps more of historical than of practical interest, over a great many years

as to whether those terms were fulfilled with respect to the provision of transportation and communication with Vancouver island.
The hon. member goes on to discuss the matter of the agreement which implied the building of a railway to Esquimalt on the southern end of Vancouver island. I hope the present Minister of Justice will be prepared to put in an oar in any discussion the cabinet has of this situation, and to point out that there is this historic responsibility on the part of the federal government to see that the people of the west coast of British Columbia have a reasonable transportation service.
Now, I gather that the hour of five o'clock has arrived-

Well, that discussion took place in 1953-54, and I find that on May 27, 1954, this subject matter was again brought forward by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I had been discussing at some length the problems of the various communities along the coast, and at page 5169 I said:
Then we come back again to Texada Island which is in the gulf. There we find a situation arising out of the fact that the C.P.R. steamer service to Powell River, which had included this island as a port of call, was being withdrawn and that the residents not only of Powell River but of Texada island were not going to have any means whatever of getting their cars in and out of that area. It is perfectly true that plans had been made for the building of a road and the establishment of a car ferry which would make car and truck transport to Powell River a possibility. But we find there a situation where a service which has been provided for years is being arbitrarily withdrawn before any substitute is provided to take its place. In the last few years that sort of thing has been happening all over the coastal area.
I mention that, Mr. Chairman, to make it clear that so far as I am concerned the Canadian Pacific steamship company has had no greater degree of interest or responsibility in maintaining service than has Union Steamships or some of the other concerns to which my hon. friend the hon. member for Skeena referred in his remarks.
It being five o'clock, I shall rise so the house may discuss private and public bills.

the second reading of Bill No. 6, to amend the Canada Elections Act (voting at advance polls).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill, which I have had the privilege of presenting to the House of Commons on at least

two previous occasions, is to extend the privilege of voting at the advance poll in connection with federal elections to any qualified voter who finds that he will have to be away from home on election day for any reason whatever. As hon. members are aware, there is at present in the Canada Elections Act a provision for the holding of a certain number of advance polls. However, the right to vote at those advance polls is limited to commercial travellers, fishermen, employees on railways, vessels and aircraft, together with members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Even in connection with these categories of voters permission to vote at the advance polls is allowed only if the voter is away from home in pursuit of his employment as defined in the Canada Elections Act.
I am sure that hon. members will agree with me that one of the rather common grievances at election time, and as candidates in elections we do pick up these grievances, is the fact that many people find that they have to be away from home at election time and cannot vote because their absence is not covered by the provisions in the act. It seems to me that we should take a new look at this question; that we should be thoroughly consistent with our belief that the right to vote is a privilege which belongs to every one of our citizens.
If, then, the right to vote is a privilege, I submit that we have no right to take that privilege away from any one of our citizens if, for example, he has to be away from home because he is on vacation. I mention that type of absence in particular because it is a most common one so far as the grievances brought to our attention are concerned and I think it brings into focus the problem presented by this particular shortcoming in the Canada Elections Act. Surely it is no crime to be away on holidays. Surely one is not committing some misdemeanour for which he should suffer a penalty such as the loss of his right to vote. Either a citizen has the right to vote or he does not have that right and if he has it it seems to me that our elections act should safeguard it in every possible way.
In a number of the provinces in this country there are provisions for the universal right to vote at advance polls. This is true in my own province of Manitoba as well as in some other provinces and I know that in the province of Manitoba the fact that any one who finds he will be away from home on election day may vote at the advance poll does not result in an avalanche of votes being cast in this way. People do not take undue advantage of the advance polls; it is still only a small percentage of the population which votes in this manner, but the right or
Canada Elections Act
the privilege is there and it does remove a very serious grievance which obtains at federal elections.
In at least two provinces of this country, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, there is a provision which I think is very commendable and which is even wider. I refer to the provision for absentee voting. In each of these provinces at general election time it is possible for a person to vote if he is away from home anywhere in the province. Arrangements are made for him to make his choice among the candidates of his own constituency and then, by the machinery which has been set up, these votes are counted and added to the total of votes for the candidates in the home constituency. In other words, what is done with regard to civilian absentees at provincial elections in Saskatchewan and British Columbia is the same as is done with regard to the service vote in our federal general elections. Our service personnel are in effect absent from their home constituencies but they are not denied their right to vote. Rather their votes are taken where they are and the totals for the various candidates are added to the totals of the civilian vote.
True, any arrangement of this kind involves extra machinery and involves some delay in the final totals being arrived at but surely it is of the essence of democracy that everyone who is a qualified voter-in other words everyone who is qualified by virtue of age, citizenship and residence in the country -should have the right to exercise that vote. Furthermore that vote should not be taken away from him because the election happens to fall at a time when he has to be away, whether it be on some kind of business not covered by the act or whether it be because he is on a holiday.
I have referred again to the question of holidays because, as I say, that is the cause of the greatest number of grievances in this field and I submit that since the time when the elections act was first drafted in this country there has been a great change both in the attitude towards the taking of holidays and in the number of people who are able to take holidays. Because of these changes I submit it is time for a change in the act itself.
My bill, since it is a bill, must therefore be a complete entity in itself and it goes into many details. However, most of those details -indeed all of them-are consequential upon the basic change which is proposed. That basic change-the principle of the bill and the only change which is now before the house for consideration-is the question as to whether voting at the advance polls should be limited to the few employment categories

Canada Elections Act
to which I have already referred or whether it should be made available to all those who are qualified voters. There is in the bill as I have had it drafted a provision that before a person could qualify to vote at an advance poll he would have to take an affidavit in which he would declare that he believes he will be away from home on election day. The reason does not have to be stated. In other words, any reason is sufficient so long as the voter is prepared to declare by way of an affidavit that he believes he will be away from home on election day.
This does not mean that it is a false affidavit if it turns out later that the voter is not away from home and I know that is the sort of thing that happens, for example in my province of Manitoba, where voting at advance polls is open to all qualified voters. I mention that detail just to make it clear that there is that one particular provision which imposes some limitation. In other words, a person has at least to be in the position of being able to give an affidavit to the effect that the believes he will be away from home on election day.
I hope the members who study this bill and speak to it will not get involved-first because it would be out of order to discuss the clauses of the bill in any case and, second, because these matters of detail do get away from the principle-in some of the consequential changes which are set out in the bill and which are necessary, either in the form in which they are spelled out in the bill or in some other form, on account of this principal change. In other words, if you are going to have the universal right to vote at advance polls it would follow that more people than at present will vote at these advance polls and, in the opinion of our election officials, that would seem to make necessary a longer lapse of time between the day when the advance polls close and the day when the general election is held. If there is going to have to be a longer lapse of time -not necessarily the length of time mentioned in my bill but some additional length of time-it may also be necessary to put the official nomination day a little further ahead of election day than is now the case.
However, Mr. Speaker, these are details which do not affect the basic principle of the bill; they can be changed one way or another, or the committee on privileges and elections to which I hope this bill will be referred after second reading might decide that these changes are not necessary at all and that it would be possible to carry out the idea of the universal right to vote at advance polls even with the other provisions of the act as they now stand.

There has been a great deal of conjecture as to when the next election is coming. On a number of occasions, we have had it in the middle of the summer, right in the midst of the vacation period when the number of people who would have wished to vote at advance polls would, I believe, have been very large. Current rumour suggests that the election might not be held off until the summer, that it might be held on April 14 or during the third or fourth week in March. If it comes on dates of this description there would, of course, not be many people away on holiday, but there would still be people who would lose their right to vote because they would be absent from home, people in addition to those listed in the present act. But if there is to be an election in the early spring, that might give us a chance to try out this idea of giving a greater number of people the right to vote at advance polls before we experiment with the idea in the middle of summer, perhaps at the election after next, when the numbers away on vacation would be greater.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary for me to argue further as to the merits of the principle of this bill. I urge hon. members not to become bogged down in details because none of the details is sacrosanct; any of them can be altered in the committee of privileges and elections. I recall the discussions that took place on the estimates of the Secretary of State (Mrs. Fairclough) earlier this session, and hon. members in many quarters of the house, fresh from the election of June 10, complained that nothing had yet been done about widening the privilege of voting at advance polls. Here is an opportunity to approve of the principle that any qualified voter should have the right to vote at an advance poll, and I say at this time that if this bill is given second reading I will not ask that it go immediately to the committee of the whole but will move that it be referred to the committee on privileges and elections so that it may be examined and changed if necessary to meet the wishes of members generally at that time.
Mr. Speaker, I hope it will not seem to be lacking in tact if as a clinching argument in support of my bill I refer once again to the fact that in the election campaign preceding the election of June 10 there was in one constituency of this country a most excellent piece of election literature. I refer to a well set-up four page leaflet put out in the constituency of St. Paul's by the Progressive Conservative association. I am not surprised that the candidate supported in this four-page election leaflet won his election, and indeed it gives me pleasure once again to

refer to him with esteem as our first commoner. I will not refer to the other items which are mentioned in this excellent piece of literature distributed on your behalf, sir, but I should like to read this sentence which appears on page four:
If you are a commercial traveller, an airline pilot or stewardess, a railway employee or a sailor you may vote in the advance poll from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m., Thursday, Friday and Saturday, June 6, 7 and 8.
Then I ask the house to note the next sentence which is in parenthesis:
Sorry, but Liberal government regulations will not permit advance poll for vacationers.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that if you are a candidate, as I trust you will be, in the next election it will not be necessary for your campaign committee in the leaflet to be prepared at that time on your behalf to put in the same sentence changing the words to read: "Sorry, but Conservative government regulations will not permit advance poll for vacationers."
I admit this is bordering on something which perhaps should not be done, that is bringing Your Honour into a debate, but I tried to do it with somewhat the same sense of humour which Your Honour uses on occasions. In that spirit it has been a pleasure to quote that complaint against the former Liberal government for not having agreed to this change in the hope that this new House of Commons will look with favour on the principle of this bill.
I say again that though there may be details about which there could be argument, let us have those arguments in committee. The only question before us is whether or not the right to vote at advance polls should be limited to commercial travellers, fishermen, employees on railways, vessels, aircraft and so on and members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or whether that right should be extended to any Canadian voter who finds that he or she will have to be away from home on election day for any reason whatsoever. After all, the right to vote is a privilege, and being away on holiday is not a crime for which any person should suffer any disability as far as his rights of citizenship are concerned. I feel that the right to vote at advance polls should be extended to all qualified voters, and it is on that basis that I present this bill to the house for second reading.

Mr. Speaker, we listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and to his suggestion that we should discuss the principle of extending the rights of voters to vote. It would seem to me that if
Canada Elections Act
we were to follow his argument to a logical conclusion we might say we all agree we should eliminate a cold or something of that sort, and according to that principle, that we should accept the first remedy offered. I suggest that that reasoning cannot very well be followed in dealing with a bill affecting so many people, introduced without the benefit of advice from those who are primarily concerned with the administration of the election act, and without the benefit of a much fuller discussion than would be possible during the time remaining in this session for the discussion of private members' bills.
I suggest to you, sir, that the hon. member who introduced this bill cannot have been too serious about what he actually did say, because he has introduced and put on the order paper so many other bills, and if one took seriously that he really means that this bill should be passed this session, then he would have put this bill on the order paper so that it could have come up the required number of times on private members' days and so that it could have had the full discussion it merits, instead of putting on the order paper a great many other bills which also must have full and proper discussion.
As to the principle of enlarging the franchise at the advance polls to all voters, I think that if the house will refer to the remarks of the Secretary of State (Mrs. Fair-clough) when her estimates were under discussion hon. members will see that she agrees with the principle that it should be enlarged.
The bill goes a little further than the hon. member would suggest it goes. He said the amendments are merely consequential to the general principle. One small amendment he advocates is advancing the date of official nomination from two to three weeks. That could effectively eliminate certain candidates from elections. There are many people who for personal, financial or other reasons cannot be persuaded to enter the public field until a very short period of time immediately prior to election day and the adoption of the hon. member's amendment would eliminate that group from public service. I do not suppose the hon. member who introduced the bill considered for one moment that that would be the effect of it nor did he entertain any thought of having it achieve that effect but that is a consideration of which we must take note of in this house.
He suggested we do not read the bill before dealing with it. I admit I read the bill rather casually but one provision I observed suggests that the advance poll is going to be counted before the results of the general voting day are known. If those results are known to individuals they could

Canada Elections Act
have a serious effect on the general vote and not necessarily a proper one. It would be something like running an advance poll in each polling subdivision, and to have the vote counted some days ahead of time more than one person would know the result as they must because each candidate would be entitled to have his agent present at the count. This would result in an advance indication of the feeling of the people who voted which would in some way have an effect on the people who came to vote on election day. We must look at this bill. We must not take the medicine that is prescribed without examining what we are taking. This course of action is what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests should be followed.
If a proper bill amending the Canada Elections Act were introduced and referred to a commitee another subject that might be discussed is the cost of advance polls. I do not think cost is of primary importance among the considerations to be discussed in determining whether or not advance polls should be held but since we are dealing with the public purse these days it might be interesting to hon. members to appreciate that if this bill is passed and advance polls are created we would be dealing with an expenditure of approximately $250,000. This is a matter we have to take under advisement with regard to the principle in question but there are other things with which I think we can agree.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests that all people entitled to the franchise should be allowed to vote. He neglected to include in his remarks consideration [DOT] of the people who serve this country so well overseas in the foreign service. There is no provision in the bill for granting the right to vote to these people, the absentee votes such as he described in Saskatchewan and British Columbia. If the hon. member is sincere in saying he wants all Canadians who are entitled to vote to have a vote then this bill is singularly lacking in a provision for those who are serving this country in a civilian capacity outside the country. If we are going to deal with amendments to the Canada Elections Act then we should deal with them right across the board and not on a piecemeal basis.
There are several other things we might consider. In this short session we have experienced two by-elections and have sat looking at the seat of the hon. member to be wondering exactly what day he would appear. I think an amendment that would permit a member to take his seat immediately following the by-election subject to the formalities
[Mr. PaUett.l
being completed after he has taken his seat would be desirable. I came to this house by a by-election in 1954. My riding was without a representative for some months before that election was called and it was some weeks after the election before I was able to take my seat here. I see that the hon. mem-for the Yukon is not yet with us. That riding has been without representation for some months. I suggest this is another thing that could be considered in a general review of the Canada Elections Act.
I have heard it said that we might become more realistic about the expenses of elections and that we should do as they do in England and set out that no more than a certain amount of money may be spent in a riding in the conduct of an election campaign. It has also been suggested that we should make some provision in the laws of the country so that financial contributions to the political life of the country, and after all that is a vibrant part of the country, should receive some consideration in the form of being allowable expenses or something of that sort. Would it be desirable to establish a maximum of a certain amount on the money that can be spent in an election in any given riding? These are things that a review of the act might well disclose.
If we want to follow the principle enunciated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre of enlarging the scope of the act to extend the privilege of voting to all those who are entitled to vote we would have to consider the taking of votes in hospitals and allowing invalids certain privileges at the polls. There are many things we would have to consider if we are to extend the franchise and I think every hon. member of this house would agree that the right to vote should be made available to every Canadian both inside or outside the country.
In my own law office I have had the experience of taking the vote of United States citizens who were in this country. They were voting in Canada in elections which were taking place in the United States. They were absentee voters. They had forms which they filled out and affidavits which were sworn, and they were allowed to vote in Canada or, for that matter, anywhere in the world, in elections taking place in the United States. I think it is a very desirable thing. It gave them a pride in their country. It gave them an opportunity to participate in the events that were taking place on that day.
We agree, Mr. Speaker, with the general idea of enlarging the franchise. That has been done, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, in many provinces.

I do not agree with the suggestion that we can deal with this bill, which 1 am sure the hon. member knew full well could not have a full discussion because so many other bills have been placed on the order paper, and which, his plea notwithstanding, I have read and found to be lacking in many respects. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the proper course for this house to follow is the course followed in connection with the bill introduced by the government, when with the advice of those people who are handling the election machinery, with the advice of the committee on privileges and elections-on which I had the honour to sit along with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which dealt very fully with this problem in 1955 and which at that time, as matters were then explained to the committee, decided not to endorse this proposal. It may be, of course, that times have changed enough so that the committee might feel that it is now opportune to advance it. These are matters that the house should know. It should know that on a reference of this matter to the committee that was the conclusion that was reached.
We have to consider all these things, Mr. Speaker, and not just one member's remarks that this is the principle, that this is the sugar-coated candy that will cure the ailments. Let us take this sugar coat off the candy and examine it. When we do we shall find that it is not a bill that effectively does what the member wants it to do or what he hopes it will do. It is not a bill that the members of this house, I am sure, feel will enlarge the franchise to the extent that every member here wishes it to do. If we are to extend the vote to everyone-and that is a desirable thing, Mr. Speaker-I suggest we have the legislation set out in language that we can support.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill to amend the Canada Elections Act. I cannot help but admire the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and his persistence in year after year bringing this question of advance polls to our attention. The question of voting, whether it be at advance polls or at any other poll that takes place, or on the regular polling day, is of great importance to us in Canada. It is a privilege that was won for us with great eloquence and persistence by our forefathers and is something of which we should be justly proud. I believe that every Canadian is proud of that right, the right to take a part in the affairs of his country, through the medium of the ballot, the medium of being allowed to vote on election day.
Canada Elections Act
When the question of advance polls was discussed on the estimates of the Secretary of State (Mrs. Fairclough) I made the statement that I was in favour of enlarging the scope of those who are permitted to vote at advance polls for the simple reason, Mr. Speaker, that we are living in changing times, in times when transportation facilities have made it possible for people to live many miles away from their work. We have construction workers who, through skills that they have and positions that they occupy, do not work in the same municipality-some of them do not work in the same province-in which they live. Many of them have to leave home early on Monday morning and do not return home until late on Friday evening. The result is that when election day comes along they have their wages to make and even though they are allowed a short time in which to cast their ballots, many times they have to leave home before the polls open. The result is that they are not allowed to exercise their franchise. In fact there are people who drive 80 to 90 miles a day to their work, day in and day out, with the result that it is sometimes a tremendous hardship for them to exercise that franchise which is so important to the people of Canada. Consideration should be given to this.
When the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) was speaking he said many things about the election act which would bear investigation and revision. No doubt this question of advance polls is one that should be given considerable attention. We do know that in 1951 the act was amended and no doubt then and, as the hon. member for Peel indicated, in 1955 consideration was given to the question. However, this bill which indicates that practically anybody who for any reason whatsoever is away from home on election day, or intends to be away from home on election day, can vote gives a little too much scope to people. It would allow them to vote at whatever time they wished. I sometimes feel that in the last election we had enough indication of what could happen in the way of impersonation and unfair election practices during election day. If this amendment were made to the Canada Elections Act we would have instead of one election day probably three or four election days. What would be the result? This day is, as I indicated, so important to the people of Canada.
It is the day in which the individual citizen can take his part and his share in welding and developing the principles and the rules of law that are so important to this country. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre indicated that there is a lot of discussion

Canada Elections Act
about the lack of interest on election day but if we had three or four election days on which practically anybody whose name was an the voter's list could vote I think the importance of election day would certainly be lessened. People would say, "well, I can vote on Thursday, Friday or Saturday of the week before." The result would be that more people would say, "Well, what is the use? It is not important." They would not bother to vote.
I think election day is too important from the point of view of Canada's welfare and history to alter the present situation too much and widen the scope to the extent that the bill before us does. If we are going to have several election days then, as the hon. member for Peel indicated, we would have a duplication of the services that are necessary on election day. Instead of having a few advance polls we would have many, with all the officers necessary to control those polls, and the result would be that expenses would mount and the cost to the country would be a great deal more than it is now. Goodness knows, we hear enough now about the tremendous cost of elections, and if we were to provide for additional days of voting at advance polls I think it would add tremendously to the cost of elections.
As I indicated, I believe that something should be done to widen the scope in order to make it possible for more people to vote who have to work away from home on election day. But I do not believe that people who want to go hunting or fishing on election day should be allowed to go to an advance poll a few days before, sign an affidavit and vote. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I cannot support the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to express a few thoughts before this resolution is carried. One of them has to do with the words the hon. minister used in making his announcement this afternoon when he explained to the house that he had registered a vigorous protest against the United States limitations on the import of oil to that country from Canada. I note, and I think all of us do, that this is not the first time in recent years that the United States government has placed limitations on the import of Canadian products, and the present Minister of Finance when he was in opposition listed these instances for us on July 14, 1955 where, according to page 6130 of Hansard, he said:
In 1952 it took the form of restrictions on dairy imports from Canada; in 1953, more restrictions on dairy imports; in 1954, quotas on imports of Canadian oats b.arley and rye; and in 1955, steps to curtail imports on crude oil from Canada, and hardboard, and the issue there is still in the balance.
We have more recently had warning that there may be curtailment of Canadian exports of lead and zinc to the United States. This process has been going on for some time now and may become much more serious in the years ahead, and I feel that careful consideration by this committee of exactly what the

Interim Supply
minister meant when he spoke of a vigorous protest is very warranted. The former minister of trade and commerce made several replies as to what he was doing with regard to the situation. On July 14, 1955, in reply to the present Minister of Finance, Mr. Howe said on page 6166:
Our representations have been made, and we are hopeful that there will be no change in the tariff on hardboard.
These words have a familiar ring when we think of the words of the Minister of Finance this afternoon. Then, on page 5621 on July 4, 1955, the present Minister of Finance gave some indication that he was not satisfied with the type of reply he was receiving, and he said:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce what action the government proposes to take in view of the latest United States steps to exclude Canadian rye.
It is obvious that the present Minister of Finance was expecting the government of the day to inform the house as to what action it was intending to take. That is precisely what the Canadian people are now asking him to do. On another occasion the former minister of trade and commerce, Mr. C. D. Howe, made this statement as recorded in Hansard of December 14, 1953 at page 862:
It has been the hope of the Canadian government that the United States government would in its own interest and in the interest of the free world decide not to impose any further restrictions on imports.
This was over four years ago, Mr. Chairman, but it seems by now to be obvious to all of us that the hopes which the Right Hon. C. D. Howe then entertained have not been borne out by the facts, because since then, as I mentioned previously, there have been limitations placed on the export of various Canadian products. As recorded on page 277 of Hansard of November 24, 1953, the hon. member for Middlesex East asked the government this:
What about suggesting to the United States that they honour their signature to the Geneva and subsequent agreements? ... Is the policy of the government again to be too little and too late?
We are now, in the light of our serious marketing difficulties, asking the hon. member for Eglinton, now that he is Minister of Finance and the man responsible, whether he is going to be responsible for a government policy which is going to do too little and be too late.
When I think of the nature of his reply this afternoon I cannot resist reading back to him something he had to say about another government some time ago on March 18, 1954, at which time the government of

the day was not very clear in stating its intentions to parliament. He said on that occasion, as recorded at page 3130 of Hansard:
The minister's answers were evasions; but the time for evasion has passed, the time for a statement of policy from the government has come-
I feel very keenly that simply registering a vigorous protest is not enough. I am not blaming the government of the United States for following the policies it is following. It has to listen to the voice of the people. It also has elections which it must face and the United States government, unless there are more powerful reasons for not doing so, will pay attention to the lobbyists in that country, will pay attention to the voters it has to face at election time. In fact some of the actions of the United States government which at times have not been very helpful to Canadian producers are not to be condemned at all. As the hon. member for Acadia pointed out so well this afternoon, and as he has pointed out on other occasions, the United States government at least has found a way of making surpluses available to those people in the world who require those things which that country has in surplus. The United States government is taking the action it has taken because of the weakness of the Canadian government both past and present.
If the Canadian government were able to convince the United States government that its vigorous protests were something more than mere words then the government of that country would consider the consequences. As it is the United States government does not have to pay any attention to us. It knows we will only continue to make vigorous protests. We will make representations, as the former minister of trade and commerce used to say, and we will let it go at that and our people are bound to suffer the hardship of unemployment that results when we lose markets.
The Canadian government has it within in its power to make the United States government pay attention to what it says. We have south of the border a customer that must have our asbestos, nickel and cobalt and that for defence purposes requires air fields in Canada. The United States requires various other concessions and certainly it needs our co-operation. The hon. member for Vancouver East pointed out this afternoon that one way in which the government could make a vigorous protest that would have some meaning would be to put severe limitations on the importation into Canada of United States refined petroleum products. I believe that even today we are importing more petroleum products than we are exporting and if I am not mistaken a very large portion comes to us

from the United States. This is one way in which we could give the United States a very direct answer.
The other matter I wish to take up deals with nuclear bombs in the air over Canadian territory. I understood that the Minister of National Defence was going to answer the question I asked the other day of the acting minister. As yet I have not had an adequate answer to this problem which is of concern to the people of Canada. I should like to know if the government of the United States has asked the permission of the Canadian government to carry nuclear weapons across our territory and, if so, has our Canadian government given such permission? If it has given such permission what safety measures are there and what assurance have the Canadian people that a horrible accident will not take place? There can be no "maybe" in this matter. We simply cannot afford to have either a hydrogen or atomic bomb or any other nuclear weapon accidentally fall on any of our Canadian towns or cities. I understand from a fairly reliable authority that regardless of the precautions that may be taken the danger of accident exists and I feel the government owes the Canadian people an assurance in this respect.
I was very pleased to hear the announcement made this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that we are giving some aid to Ceylon. In that connection I should like to quote again the remarks of the present Minister of Finance when he was in opposition on November 18, 1953, at page 139 of Hansard. Dealing with the subject of aid to the underdeveloped nations of the world the hon. member for Eglinton said there are areas in the world today where people are hungry and he went on to quote Mr. Trygve Lie who is supposed to have said:
There is no fact In the world, in terms of humanity and in terms of politics, which is more important than this:	The vast majority of the
people of the world live in poverty and misery and they know it and they don't like it. Most human beings are hungry today most of the time; more than half the people in the world are illiterate; half of the world population is constantly ill, and expected to die before the age of 35.
The hon. member for Eglinton then went on at some length to impress upon the government the urgent need to supply such countries as India, Pakistan and Ceylon with some of their basic needs and he referred specifically to the large supply of surplus wheat we have. As reported at page 140 of Hansard of that date he went on to say:
We should go forward and say, "We are going to help you; we are going to help to feed you, and we are going to do it in a way that will strike the imagination of the eastern world, we hope of the entire world."
Interim Supply
Unfortunately for the poor people of Ceylon there has been presented to us a splendid chance for the Minister of Finance to show the people of Canada that he meant what he said on this matter back in 1953. To send just medicine and take other such measures in terms of assisting Ceylon is unworthy of the wealth of this nation. The government proposes sending merely one, two or three airplanes loaded with supplies for 300,000 homeless refugees. I should like to recommend that we send a shipload of lumber, lumber which is in excess supply on the west coast, in order to build some homes for these 300,000 refugees or homeless people and that we offer to the government of Ceylon, let us say, one million bushels of wheat of which we have so many millions of bushels in excess supply. Ceylon is a sister nation of the commonwealth, a democracy, a new nation. And Ceylon has a fairly powerful communist party. Let us not again sit back with a policy of too little and too late and wait until Soviet Russia has made an offer to the people of Ceylon.
We could make the offer this very evening that if they could use it we will supply them with enough lumber to build their houses and with enough wheat to feed those people until they are able to plant those fields again and raise their own food. It would help us in providing employment for all our people on the west coast and in other lumbering areas. It would help Canadian agriculture; it would help us in our ideological battle against communism.
However, I do not think we should be making the offer because of those reasons and they are valid reasons in themselves. It is only right that we who have more than we need should share with those who have met with this disaster. For this reason and this reason alone we should make the offer and I appeal to the government to make such an offer to the government of Ceylon before another 24 hours roll by. Let it for once be a democracy that is ahead of the game in this ideological war.
