speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this morning I intended to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs a question regarding the decision made by the government to aid Ceylon. The Secretary of State for External Affairs made a statement before I had a chance to ask him the question but, like the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I was very disappointed that the national emergency

Interim Supply
in Ceylon should have been treated as it was this morning. I was sorry that the new Secretary of State for External Affairs was not able to announce that on hearing of this calamity he immediately cabled the prime minister of Ceylon offering assistance on behalf of the Canadian people. I feel very strongly about this question because I, along with 12 other Canadians, was the guest of the government of Ceylon a few weeks ago. At this point I should like to thank the hon. members of my own party and the Canadian Branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association for making it possible for the Canadian delegation to attend the first commonwealth parliamentary conference that has ever been held in Asia. Three countries acted as hosts: Ceylon, Pakistan and India, and about 100 delegates from all parts of the commonwealth enjoyed the wonderful hospitality extended to us by our hosts in this important part of the world.
Naturally, on Christmas day, when I heard that Ceylon was experiencing the most serious floods that they had ever had in the 2,500 years of recorded history of that very beautiful island, I hoped that Canada would rise to the occasion in a generous way. The first day's reports indicated that 94 people had lost their lives. The next day the total was up to 130 and the last report I saw indicated that 288 had lost their lives and about half as many people as we have in the province of Saskatchewan are homeless, having lost their worldly possessions and their future is uncertain because of those terrible floods. The neighbouring countries have responded very generously, and I am glad that Canada has done something. But to draw from the defence stores medical supplies and foods in a crisis of this sort does not really represent the feelings of the majority of the Canadian people.
I share the view of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that the Minister of Finance, who expressed those very generous sentiments after he had attended a commonwealth parliamentary conference and got first-hand information regarding conditions in some parts of the commonwealth, would want to review the statement made by his colleague this morning and to have something more generous placed on the record tomorrow.
While I am on my feet I should like to take a few moments to report on the part that Canada is playing in this part of the world. In Ceylon we were told of the work that has been done in the co-operative movement by Canadians who received their training at St. Francis Xavier in Nova Scotia. There are six very important co-op centres that have been set up as a result of Canadian contributions under the Colombo plan. We

heard a good deal of Mr. Gus. McDonald, who received his training at St. Francis Xavier. Although it is six or seven years since Mr. McDonald was there, for the next 25 years his name is going to be a name that will be highly regarded. When they have a difficult problem in the vegetable co-ops, for example, one of the members says: "Well, now, if Mr. McDonald was here he would suggest that we approach this problem in this way. He would not approve of the suggestions that have been made by one of the members," and whoever can express the considered opinion of what Mr. McDonald would do in a given situation carries a good deal of influence.
Naturally, we were pleased to hear of the part that the Canadian homemakers and women's institutes have played in improving the standard of living of their sister women in Ceylon. Lady Coomer Aswamy, the wife of the high commissioner designate from Ceylon to Canada, has been very active in organizing the country women of Ceylon. We saw her report and noted with some pride that Canada was right at the top of the list of contributors and had made a more generous contribution to the work of keeping the country women of Ceylon than rich countries such as the United States and Great Britain. I am sure that during the lifetime of all the people in Ceylon the fact that Canadian women who have never been to Ceylon have been willing to make investments in order that there might be nursery education, health centres, and classes in home management to make life a little more tolerable for the people of that area, will be greatly appreciated.
We did not see Professor Hardy, a very distinguished professor, from the University of Saskatchewan. He has been in Ceylon now for several years under F.A.O. When I learned that Canada contributes a little over two cents per person per year to the work of F.A.O. I realized that Professor Hardy has been able to go out there and spend six years to help introduce new methods of cultivation in that area. I feel that Canadians generally should have the opportunity to know more of the work that is being done by some of our Canadians who go out under schemes such as W.H.O. and F.A.O. and other schemes promoted by specialized agencies of the United Nations.
' I realize that while we have so many unsolved problems in Canada, governments do receive criticism for spending any money outside the country; but when one realizes that for two cents per person per year a man with Professor Hardy's outlook on life, his background-he has been president of

the trustees association of Saskatchewan; he was an outstanding rugby player when he was much younger than he is now-, with all his vast experience, can go to that part of the world and start life over again when he had an assured future in the province among his friends, is something for which Canadians have reason to be proud.
In Pakistan we had the good fortune to meet some of the Canadians who are working on the Warsak power project. Again, we were proud of the fact that these young engineers had gone out there with their wives and children in order to provide power and irrigation projects for the people in that area. We also met a group of engineers in Pakistan who had spent some months in Canada under the Colombo plan studying the operations of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways. While they naturally appreciated the know-how they were able to obtain from their study of our railways, the thing I remember most is the tribute they paid to the rank and file of the Canadian people. They said they could not get over the fact that when they sat down in a restaurant in Winnipeg, Calgary, Vancouver, Moncton or wherever it might be, Canadians, recognizing that they were strangers, came to their table and said, "We see you are strangers. Where is your home and what are you doing here?" Before they knew what had happened they had formed new friends and Canadian people had taken them to their homes.
It does not require a great deal of effort to take a person from another country into your home once in one's lifetime but it does mean a great deal to people who are in a strange country and away from their friends to find that they are accepted, given a chance to meet our people and to see something of home life in Canada by visiting the homes of complete strangers. Naturally we were quite thrilled to have this tribute paid to the rank and file of Canadians. These engineers did not remember any names and we were not asked to bring messages to any people who had entertained them but they were greatly impressed by the generosity of complete strangers who did not want anything from them but merely wanted their stay to be as pleasant as possible.
Naturally we spent a major part of our time in India where the commonwealth parliamentary association met for the first time in the capital of that country. This is a very important part of the world. One cannot realize the problems that exist without actually going there. We had read about these countries during our school days, but it is hard for us to realize, for example, that a million babies are born every month and that
Interim Supply
in sixteen months time as many babies are born in India as the total population of Canada.
India is embarking on a program to provide education for all children between the ages of 6 and 14. How many children are there in this age group? There are over 60 million, nearly four times as many as the entire population of Canada. They are going to have a host of problems for years to come. I think it was two weeks ago yesterday that some of our delegates visited one of the villages where 100 children met in one school, half of them in the morning and half of them in the afternoon. In this school there are no doors, windows or floors. The children sit on sacks on the ground with their legs crossed and only have a very small blackboard, but in many of these villages the children are receiving an education for the first time in the history of the country.
In one of the schools the teacher explained that the school was being conducted on the parliamentary basis. They had a prime minister and ministers of agriculture, education and health. We asked to meet the prime minister. A little lad twelve years of age came to the side of the school where we stood and explained that it was his duty to see that his colleagues discharged their respective responsibilities. We asked to see the minister of health. He had to see that the children had their faces and hands washed before they came to school. We then asked to see the minister of education. She was the most beautiful minister of education I have ever seen, with jet black eyes and braids down her back. She was only ten years old but she was emphasizing the importance of having good books in the school, of having the blackboard cleaned every morning before school started and seeing that the school was as tidy and the children as orderly as possible. I am sure that in 10 or 15 years time these children, who have only known what school is like for two years, are going to be taking a very important part in the life of that country.
Two days previously we had gone to Agra to the Taj Mahal. Hundreds of years ago 20,000 people worked for nearly 20 years to construct one of the most beautiful buildings I have seen. It is truly one of the seven wonders of the world. The people who worked on the project travelled miles from their peasant homes and worked long hours. When they finished they did have one of the most beautiful buildings in the world but I am sure that the peasants of today who see their children having the chance to go to school are getting a great deal more satisfaction out of the achievements of

Interim Supply
modern India than their great grandfathers did years ago by participating in the building of this great structure.
In India and in China to the north important experiments are under way. Both countries are fighting the ancient enemies of mankind, ignorance, disease and poverty. China has adopted communist techniques and is following a totalitarian pattern but in India the people are determined to work out a solution of their problems by the parliamentary system and democratic methods. I think it is very important that those of us in more fortunate areas of the world should appreciate more fully the importance of the experiments in this part of the world. Since we pride ourselves on belonging to a commonwealth of nations concerned about the common good, I do not think we can indefinitely accept a situation where in a country like Canada we have an average income 40 or 50 times as high as the people of India. We accept the fact that a baby born in Canada can expect to live to be 65 or 70 but we have not accepted the responsibility of seeing that the know-how that has made it possible to extend our life expectancy is made available to other countries. The life expectancy in some of these areas in Asia is less than half what it is in Canada. Hollywood has been successful in conveying the impression to Asia and Africa that this is a fairyland and that on this side of the Atlantic we have very high standards of living. Actually the standards of living are not as high as the people who see Hollywood pictures conclude but the fact is that our health records and living standards are very high. We place second to the United States, being higher than Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand, and I think a contribution of two cents per person per year to F.A.O. is not good enough in a country as rich as Canada.
The hon. member for Lanark, the leader of our delegation, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek and I had the pleasure to be present in Bombay when the first shipment of Canadian wheat was turned over to India. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek made a few brief remarks after the Canadian trade commissioner had spoken. Perhaps the Canadian people might appreciate how serious famine conditions are in that part of the world this year if they realized that rice, the staple food, cannot be used in Pakistan if more than 25 people are together at any one gathering. Rice is being rationed in parts of India. When you consider the very large supplies of wheat we have available in Canada, and the fact that Canadian wheat is prized very highly because it blends well with

wheat in that part of the world, then you realize that our most recent contribution of $7 million worth of wheat is going to create a great deal of good will. It is going to make it possible for children to live through this winter, when death would have been the alternative.
Really, this $7 million does not put a great strain on Canadian resources. I understand that is less than we spend in two days on our defence program. However, there is a limit to what 16 million people can do towards solving the problem of 360 million in India, 80 million in Pakistan and 8 million in Ceylon. I believe we could be more generous than the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs this morning would indicate in a situation where serious flood conditions have removed the life accumulations of 400,000 or 500,000 people and taken another large group to an early death. I think we could continue to participate more generously in supplying personnel to these countries.
In Bombay we met a young Canadian engineer who had only been in India for two months working on the atomic energy reactor. I was somewhat surprised to find that this young engineer said before he was in India for a week he decided he should know more about the country and its background. He decided a good book to start with would be Ghandi's autobiography. He had just finished reading over 1,000 pages and was greatly impressed by the contribution that Ghandi had made to India and to the world. Believe me, the people in India are greatly impressed by the fact that a young Canadian engineer, who has seen a great deal of the world and is not going to be in India for the rest of his life, settles down within two weeks of his arrival to try to understand more about the country and more about the people.
My last words before I sit down are to the effect that I believe we must find ways and means in the future of making it possible for more members of parliament to visit other parts of the commonwealth. I understand that since the last election two ministers have been around the world in a government plane. The former minister of national health and welfare went around the world about a year ago. He took some press correspondents with him, and I do not criticize that. I think the correspondents for Canadian newspapers should get a chance to see the world. We are living now in a very small world. I think it is unfortunate that of the 13 Canadians who went as delegates, not one had been outside Canada before on any mission of this sort.
Since we have had a large measure of agreement in parliament here over the years on the importance of the Colombo plan, and

the role that Canada should play towards creating a better understanding, I think that when a government plane is flying all the way around the world it would not be unreasonable if the cabinet ministers concerned were to take a couple of private members from the government side and from the opposition and the Senate. We had two government members in our delegation, two members of the official opposition, one from the Social Credit and one from this party, and a member of the Senate. I believe a delegation of that size might reasonably be taken on these important trips to international meetings of the World Health Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization, meetings of the Colombo plan, and so on.
As conditions in Canada become more difficult there is going to be more criticism about using funds outside of Canada while we have so many unsolved problems in this country. I do not believe, in this critical period of the world's history, any country can wait until all domestic problems are solved before participating more actively in solving the problems of the commonwealth and of the whole world. I make a special plea, therefore, to the Minister of Finance, who had the good fortune to go to Africa when he was a private member, to use his good offices to see that when government planes are flying around the world at public expense consideration is given to having an all-party delegation go along so that the elected representatives of the people will be able to give first-hand information to their people back home regarding the importance of Canada participating in solving these complicated national and international problems.

speechtext: Order. Department of National Defence, Vote 240. The item will be found on page 47 of the Blue Book, details on page 313. On Thursday, December 5, last, when this matter was last under discussion by the committee, general discussion had been completed and the committee was considering the details under the various headings set out on pages 313 to 315. Discussion had been concluded on the heading "Departmental Administration" and was proceeding on the heading "Inspection Services", page 315, when the committee rose. Has discussion under this heading been concluded? If so, discussion of the next heading commencing at page 318 is in order.

I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that we had completed this discussion. We were on inspection services and at that stage the minister rose to give a statement on certain savings which he had effected on various items and I was under the impression when we were drawing to a close on December 5 that the minister was to have a statement ready for the further discussion on the estimates with particular regard to those items on which such savings had been effected. I was wondering if the hon. minister would be prepared to open his discussion today on that basis.

In answer to the question which was asked on this particular item, Mr. Chairman, I was requested to state how much had been spent during the fiscal year of 1956 to 1957 on inspection services.
The amount spent was $8,088,389 out of an estimate of $10,105,000. This year, out of an estimate of $9,649,000, it is estimated that there will be an expenditure of $8,217,733. Thus in the year 1956 to 1957, there was a saving or money unspent totalling $2,016,611. This year, having taken into consideration when the estimates were prepared and the saving or the unspent money of last year, it is estimated there will be a saving of $1,431,267. This estimate of the unspent money is due to the completion of much of the procurement program and, therefore, less money is required for the inspection services.

The role of the naval reserves in Canada is to provide personnel to complete the shore and ship establishments in the event of an emergency. They would only have a secondary role as an aid to the civil power. It is anticipated that if an emergency arose many of the regular personnel of the shore establishments would at once complete the ships' complement. The ships at the present time are manned at approximately 70 per cent of their wartime complement and the rest of the personnel are on training courses and at various shore establishments. Naval reserves in the event of an emergency would then take over those shore establishments and help to complete the establishments' complement.

He referred to the possibility, under certain conditions, of defence expenditures having to be increased. He used words such as "colossal" and "gigantic". I wonder whether the Minister of National Defence has any comment to make as to which way we are going. Are we moving in the direction of reduced defence expenditures as I thought was forecast by the minister in the opening remarks on December 5, or are we moving in the direction of more gigantic expenditures as the Prime Minister indicated was a matter of apprehension when he spoke on December 21? I could hardly be expected to discuss next year's estimates while we are still discussing this year's. I do not believe I could be expected to give an answer concerning the size of the estimates for next year. The Prime Minister indicated that there might be colossal expenditures unless certain steps were taken by the NATO countries as a whole. I hope, and I am sure the hon. member hopes as does every hon. member, that it will be possible to relieve the terrific burden which all countries are feeling so far as defence expenditures are concerned. Oil-U.S. Import Restrictions

subtopic: PRESS STATEMENT RESPECTING OIL IMPORTS INTO U.S.

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance today released the following statement:
The government of the United States has just announced that the voluntary oil import program, which has been limiting imports of oil into most parts of the United States during the past five months, will immediately be extended to include the west coast area and will thus for the first time directly affect imports from Canada. In the view of the United States, these limitations are required in order to maintain assured supplies that might be required for national defence.
The Canadian government learned with great regret, some days ago, of the United States proposal to extend import limitations. Since that time the Canadian government has made the strongest possible representations to the United States administration and has urgently pressed them to reconsider and
revise their proposals. However, in view of the mounting pressures on supply-price relationships the United States has decided that it must proceed with its plan immediately.
The United States administration has represented that the plan is not likely, in the coming months, to involve a very substantial reduction in U.S. imports from Canada below recent levels. Nevertheless the impact on Canadian interests may be expected to be adverse.
The Canadian government cannot accept the view that there is any justification for U.S. limitations on oil coming from Canada, either on economic or on defence grounds. The Canadian government will continue to press its objections.
Ottawa, December 24, 1957.

Canada-U.S.-Economic Co-operation

subtopic: EXCHANGE OF NOTES BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES

speechtext: Exchange of noies (Oclober 26, 1950) between Canada and the United Stales of America giving formal effect to the statement of principles for economic cooperation.

The Secretary of State of the United States of America to the Canadian Ambassador in the United States of America
Department of State Washington, October 26, 1950.
Excellency:
I have the honor to refer to recent discussions between representatives of our two governments for the general purpose of reaching an agreement to the end that the economic efforts of the two countries be coordinated for the common defense and that the production and resources of both countries be used for the best combined results. Their deliberations were based on concepts of economic cooperation which were inherent in the Hyde Park Agreement of 1941* and which are still valid today. They formulated and agreed to the "statement of Principles for Economic Cooperation" annexed hereto, which is intended to guide, in the light of these basic concepts, the activities of our respective governments.
If this attached statement is agreeable to your government, this note and your reply to that effect will constitute an agreement between our two governments on this subject.
Accept, Excellency, the renewed assurances of my highest consideration.

Statement of Principles for Economic Cooperation
The United States and Canada have achieved a high degree of cooperation in the field of industrial mobilization during and since World War II through the operation of the principles embodied in the Hyde Park Agreement of 1941,* through the extension of
* For the text of the agreement see Canada Treaty Series, 1941, No. 14 and Canada Treaty Series, 1948, No. 1.
its concepts in the post-war period and more recently through the work of the Joint Industrial Mobilization Planning Committee. In the interests of mutual security and to assist both governments to discharge their obligations under the United Nations Charter and the North Atlantic Treaty, it is believed that this field of common action should be further extended. It is agreed, therefore, that our two governments shall cooperate in all respects practicable, and to the extent of their respective executive powers, to the end that the economic efforts of the two countries be coordinated for the common defense and that the production and resources of both countries be used for the best combined results.
The following principles are established for the purpose of facilitating these objectives:
1.	In order to achieve an optimum production of goods essential for the common defense, the two countries shall develop a coordinated program of requirements, production and procurement.
2.	To this end, the two countries shall, as it becomes necessary, institute coordinated controls over the distribution of scarce raw materials and supplies.
3.	Such United States and Canadian emergency controls shall be mutually consistent in their objectives, and shall be so designed and administered as to achieve comparable effects in each country. To the extent possible, there shall be consultation to this end prior to the institution of any system of controls in either country which affects the other.
4.	In order to facilitate essential production, the technical knowledge and productive skills involved in such production within both countries shall, where feasible, be freely exchanged.
5.	Barriers which impede the flow between Canada and the United States of goods essential for the common defense effort should be removed as far as possible.
6.	The two governments, through their appropriate agencies, will consult concerning any financial or foreign exchange problems which may arise as a result of the implementation of this agreement.

B.C. Forest Access Roads

subtopic: LETTER RESPECTING CONSTRUCTION OF FOREST ACCESS ROADS

speechtext:
Ottawa, January 2, 1958.
The Honourable W. A. C. Bennett,
Premier of the Province of British Columbia, Victoria, British Columbia.
My dear Premier:
Under the Canada Forestry Act the government of Canada has offered financial assistance to all provinces with respect to the completion and maintenance of provincial inventories of forest resources, certain kinds of reforestation projects, and, more recently, capital expenditures required for forest fire protection. Agreements relating to one or more of these classes of forestry activity have been executed with nine of the provinces.
My colleagues and I feel that the protection of the forests against fire is a matter of particular importance. Although substantial improvements have been made in this field in recent years, forest fire losses are still excessive and constitute a major deterrent to the application of sound silvicultural practices in forest management.
Good access roads are essential to the attainment of adequate forest fire protection, as well as for other forest management requirements. The seventh British commonwealth forestry conference, which recently met in Australia and New Zealand, recommended that "road systems be developed wherever necessary to permit maximum efficiency and economy in the management and protection of the forests and in the utilization of their produce".
In view of the foregoing and also in view of the need to provide additional employment this winter and spring my colleagues and I are of the opinion that the time is now opportune, if the provinces are so disposed, to enter into further agreements under the Canada Forestry Act which would provide for additional federal financial aid to the provinces for the construction of forest access roads and trails. The agreement envisaged would be essentially along the following lines:
(a)	The road and trail construction programs to which the federal government would contribute would be planned and executed by the provinces. The federal contribution would be 50 per cent of the cost,
the remainder being paid by the province or by a forest protective association.
(b)	Federal aid under this proposal would apply to expenditures incurred between the date of this letter and June 30, 1958, and the maintenance of roads and trails would be a provincial responsibility.
(c)	The forest access roads and trails included in such programs would be those required for forest fire protection excluding, of course, county or municipal roads and provincial highways.
(d)	Projects to which Canada would contribute under the proposed agreement would not be eligible for assistance under the present fire protection agreement with respect to costs incurred during the period referred to above. However, any unfinished work on such projects, on and after July 1, 1958, would be eligible for inclusion in programs under the present agreement. The latter provides for a federal share of road and trail construction costs amounting to 25 per cent, subject of course to a total yearly allotment.
(e)	Provinces may include their share of the costs under the proposed agreement-to the extent properly chargeable to fire protection-in calculating their annual expenditures on fire protection for the purpose of arriving at allotments of federal contributions under the present agreement.
(f)	Canada would not make any contribution with respect to the acquisition of any land or right of way.
I should be glad of your views on this proposal, and of your advice at the earliest possible date as to whether an agreement along the lines indicated above would be acceptable to the government of your province. In the event that it does prove acceptable, a preliminary estimate of the cost of the program you envisage would also be appreciated.
In the meantime, if you wish your officials to obtain further details as to the agreement we might propose, they might contact Mr. J. D. B. Harrison, director of the forestry branch of this department. I have asked him to work out the detailed terms of a possible agreement under the general terms mentioned above.
Yours sincerely,
Alvin Hamilton.
Saturday, January 4, 1958
